query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the degree of local chemical short-range order (SRO) in a single-phase high-entropy alloy creates nanoscale energy barriers that hinder dislocation motion, thereby elevating hardness and yield strength compared to a fully disordered state.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized equiatomic high-entropy alloy with minimal short-range order, achieved by rapid quenching from a solution-annealing temperature.
generation.intervention: Expose the same alloy to controlled thermal treatments, incrementally varying temperature and dwell time, followed by rapid or slow cooling, to induce different levels of local chemical ordering.
generation.conditions: All samples are tested at room temperature. Microstructure is monitored via in situ high-resolution TEM or synchrotron XRD both before and after each thermal treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemical short-range ordered regions acting as localized barriers to dislocation glide.
generation.mechanism: Greater SRO increases the potential energy landscape for dislocations, pinning them more effectively and reducing their mobility, thus raising hardness and strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with higher degrees of SRO will exhibit up to ~10–30% higher microhardness and yield strength compared to the fully disordered baseline sample, demonstrating a direct correlation between increased ordering and mechanical strengthening.
generation.baseline: A fully disordered, solution-treated sample of the same alloy with minimal detectable short-range order.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis primarily applies to nominally single-phase multi-principal element alloys under conditions where appreciable local ordering can form. In systems with significant phase segregation or competing strengthening mechanisms (e.g., precipitation), the effect of SRO may be overshadowed.
generation.uncertainty: Other microstructural effects (e.g., grain size changes, secondary phases) may also influence mechanical properties, so disentangling the impact of SRO from these effects may require additional experiments and modeling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of equiatomic HEA samples, subjecting each to distinct thermal treatment cycles that promote different levels of chemical ordering, then measure their short-range order parameters and mechanical properties via microhardness and uniaxial testing.
measurements: Quantification of short-range order using in situ TEM or XRD techniques
Uniaxial tension or compression to determine yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured hardness and yield strength do not change in accordance with the measured degree of SRO (e.g., remain the same despite significant increases or decreases in SRO), the proposed hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials. decision.trend: Early work (PMC4682111) established that single-phase high-entropy alloys such as CrMnFeCoNi gain strength and toughness via multiple, interacting dislocation processes (including partial dislocation movement, stacking-fault formation, and dislocation pile-ups). Later studies (e.g., PMC6687833) demonstrated that local chemical ordering or short-range order formed in multi-principal element alloys can create energy barriers that impede dislocation motion and significantly enhance strength, while in other HEAs (PMC8446014, PMC11778022) the type and character of dislocations (edge versus screw) can likewise govern flow stresses. Despite progress in clarifying how local disorder and various dislocation substructures elevate strength, precisely isolating and quantifying each mechanism’s contribution to hardness remains challenging. Researchers have therefore pursued more advanced in situ nanomechanical testing, targeted compositional control (without necessarily adding new elements), and atomistic simulations to deconvolute the roles of local chemical ordering, dislocation character, and microstructure in controlling the yield stress and work-hardening behavior.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how to systematically and predictively link the evolving local chemical order, dislocation core structures, and effective lattice friction to measured hardness and strength. Consensus is lacking on how easily one might tune these features through thermomechanical processing alone. Moreover, at present only sparse data exist documenting how local ordering evolves under realistic loading conditions for different subsets of multi-principal element systems, leaving open questions about optimal processing conditions and fundamental rate-limiting mechanisms of dislocation flow in high-entropy alloys.
decision.lever: Perform high-resolution in situ TEM or X-ray diffraction on the same HEA composition subjected to controlled thermal treatments to vary local chemical ordering, then measure the corresponding changes in microhardness and yield strength while characterizing dislocation substructures in real time.
decision.why: This targeted experiment tests the hypothesis that changes in local chemical ordering create nanoscale barriers to dislocation motion, thereby governing hardness and strength. By preparing a single alloy composition and systematically adjusting thermal history to alter short-range order, one can correlate real-time observations of dislocation motion with mechanical properties. A measured increase in dislocation pinning and elevated hardness/strength after higher ordering treatments would support the hypothesis. In contrast, if controlling local order fails to alter dislocation propagation or mechanical response, the hypothesis would be falsified.
